title: New permanent residents by intended destination in 2025, and historical provincial retention
question: Where do new permanent residents intend to settle, and who remains in their intended province?
dek: Admissions describe the destination at landing; retention describes tax residence years later. They are separate measures.

findings.headline: Admissions per 1,000 residents range from 5.9 to 23.3 among comparable CMAs in 2025
findings.detail: 21 of 24 full CMAs with observed changes had fewer admissions than in 2024. The newest published year covers 2026-01 to 2026-08; partial years are not pooled with full calendar years.
findings.calc: IRCC calendar-year 2025 admissions / StatCan July 1 2025 population × 1,000; matching full-CMA geography. CA and provincial-part values are not ranked together with CMAs.

findings.headline: Provincial retention five years after admission ranges from 34% to 91%
findings.detail: Admitted 2018; tax year 2023. Ontario: 90.8%; Alberta: 86.2%; British Columbia: 84.9%; Quebec: 79.6%; Manitoba: 61.2%; Nova Scotia: 60.1%; New Brunswick: 58.5%; Saskatchewan: 47.7%; Newfoundland and Labrador: 46.5%; Prince Edward Island: 34.4%. These are province-level figures, not city rankings.
findings.calc: Publisher's Retention rate; admission year 2018, tax year 2023; total categories and ages. Stayed / (stayed + out-migrated).

charts.title: Permanent resident admissions per 1,000 — full CMAs, 2025

interpretation: A high admissions rate indicates a relatively large intended inflow, not a higher chance of eligibility or employment.
Retention does not explain why people left and excludes people who moved into the province from another initial destination.
methodology: IRCC workbook coverage: 2015-01 to 2026-08; latest complete calendar year 2025. Values rounded to five; suppressed values remain missing.
Retention uses the 2018 admission cohort in tax year 2023, from StatCan 43-10-0022-01.
Admissions per 1,000 use matching year and full-CMA July 1 population denominators; CA and CMA-part figures remain contextual.
limitations: Intended destination at landing can differ from later residence.
IRCC publishes no separate Iqaluit row; territorial retention is unavailable.
Rounding and suppression limit comparisons for small populations.
